adampur-forest.desc: Adampur, also called Kauargola forest, is one beat of the Rajkandi reserved forest in Kamalganj upazila. It is the same band of hill forest that holds Lawachara and Hamham, but far fewer people come here. Trails climb small hills through tall trees and bamboo, where you may hear gibbons and see langurs and many birds. It suits people who want a forest walk without crowds.
blocks: How to get there
From Srimangal or Kamalganj take a CNG to Adampur bazar, then walk in with a local guide.
Good to know
Hire a local guide; trails are not marked. Wear proper shoes, carry water, and watch for leeches in the rainy season.

glance: 195 km to Moulvibazar by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
goyghor-khojar-mosque.desc: This mosque was built in 1476, in the reign of Sultan Shamsuddin Yusuf Shah, by Musa ibn Haji Amir and his son Majlis Alam, the Sultan's minister in Sylhet. It sits on a little hill in Goyghor village of Mostafapur union, in what villagers say was once tiger forest, and they point to three paw marks on an inside pillar. In 1593 the Afghan chief Khwaja Usman, one of the Baro Bhuiyans, is said to have taken shelter here, which is how it got its name. The dome has been rebuilt more than once, but the very thick brick walls, the Arabic inscription near the ceiling and a stone inscription on the west wall are old.
blocks: How to get there
From Moulvibazar town take a CNG towards Mostafapur union and ask for Goyghor village; the last stretch is a village road.
Good to know
It is a working village mosque: go outside prayer times, dress modestly and ask before going in. Combine it with a tea-garden drive towards Srimangal.

srimangal-tea-museum.desc: The tea museum sits beside the Srimangal Tea Resort on the Srimangal–Bhanugach road, about 4 km from town, surrounded by tea bushes. It gathers old objects from the gardens: machines and hand tools used to process tea, along with furniture and everyday things from the British planters' era. It is a quick stop, but it helps make sense of the tea country you have been driving through.
blocks: How to get there
From Srimangal town take a CNG or auto toward Bhanugach; the museum is about 4 km east, next to the Tea Resort.
Good to know
Combine it with Lawachara National Park, which is on the same road.

glance: Village homes in Barlekha, Juri, Rajnagar and Kamalganj around Poush Sankranti in mid-January; rarely sold in shops
moulvibazar-chunga-pitha.desc: For chunga pitha, rice (often with milk, sugar or coconut) is stuffed into hollow tubes of dholu, a thin, oily bamboo that lets the rice cook through before the tube chars. The tubes are roasted slowly over straw fires on winter nights, then split open to reveal a long white roll that is sliced and eaten with fish or meat curry, or with spiced dried fish. It belongs to the hill areas of Barlekha, Juri, Rajnagar and Kamalganj, but dholu bamboo has become rare, so the pitha is now mostly made at home for guests around Poush Sankranti.

glance: 195 km to Moulvibazar by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
barshijora-eco-park.desc: Barshijora Eco Park is a protected patch of small hills on the edge of Moulvibazar town. The hillocks are thick with trees and undergrowth, with paths, picnic spots and a few cottages. Visitors heading straight to Srimangal usually skip it, so on a weekday it is quiet. It is a handy morning walk if you stay in the district town.
blocks: How to get there
From Moulvibazar town take a rickshaw or CNG to the eco park gate a few kilometres away.
Good to know
Go early for birds. Avoid walking alone deep inside on quiet days.

baikka-beel.desc: Baikka Beel is a protected fish and bird sanctuary in the Hail Haor wetland near Srimangal, managed with the local community. A watchtower overlooks open water carpeted with lotus and water lilies, where waterbirds, kingfishers and, in winter, many migratory ducks gather. It is one of the easiest wetland birdwatching sites to reach from Srimangal.
blocks: How to get there
About 45 minutes by CNG from Srimangal; the last stretch can be muddy.
Good to know
Arrive early in the morning; bring binoculars and keep noise down.

manipuri-dance.desc: The Manipuri community of Moulvibazar keeps alive a classical dance tradition of gentle, flowing movements and richly embroidered costumes, telling stories of Krishna and Radha. The highlight is the Raas Leela festival at Madhabpur in Kamalganj, held on the full moon of Kartik, usually in November, when dancers perform through the night. Manipuri weavers also produce colourful handloom shawls and fabrics sold in Srimangal and Kamalganj.
blocks: Good to know
Expect crowds at the Raas festival; dress modestly and respect the devotional setting.

glance: 195 km to Moulvibazar by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
madhabkunda-waterfall.desc: Madhabkunda is one of the best-known waterfalls in Bangladesh, dropping from a rocky cliff into a pool surrounded by forest. It flows all year but is most powerful in the rainy season. An Eco Park has been developed around it, and a short walk away is a smaller fall called Porikunda. The site is also sacred to Hindus, with a temple nearby and a bathing festival during the month of Chaitra.
blocks: How to get there
From Moulvibazar or Sylhet take a bus to Barlekha/Kanthaltoli, then a CNG to the eco park.
Good to know
Do not swim near the base or climb the rocks; the pool is deep and accidents happen.

madhabpur-lake.desc: Madhabpur Lake lies inside the Madhabpur tea estate in Kamalganj upazila. It is a man-made reservoir, formed by damming the valleys between the tea hills, so the water snakes between green slopes. In season the lake is covered with water lilies, and paths along the ridges give views over the water and the tea bushes. It is an easy half-day add-on to Srimangal or Lawachara.
blocks: How to get there
From Srimangal take a CNG toward Bhanugach/Kamalganj and on to the Madhabpur tea estate; the ride is roughly an hour.
Good to know
Go in the morning or late afternoon. The estate is a working tea garden, so keep to the paths and don't pick leaves.

lawachara-national-park.desc: Lawachara is a protected semi-evergreen forest near Srimangal, best known for its endangered western hoolock gibbons, whose loud whooping calls carry across the trees in the morning. Marked trails of different lengths lead through towering trees and bamboo, and you may also see langurs, macaques and many birds. A railway line runs through the forest, a scene made famous in the film 'Around the World in 80 Days'. A Khasi village lies within the park.
blocks: How to get there
About 15–20 minutes by CNG from Srimangal on the Kamalganj road.
Good to know
Go early and quietly to hear gibbons. Hire a park guide for longer trails. Never feed the animals.

glance: Srimangal bazar and roadside stalls on the Kamalganj road
srimangal-pineapple.desc: Besides tea, the hillocks around Srimangal and Kamalganj are planted with pineapple, and the summer harvest fills local markets with fruit. The pineapples are known for their sweetness and are sold by the piece from roadside stalls. Lemons and other fruits from the same hills are also local favourites.

srimangal-tea-gardens.desc: Srimangal is often called the tea capital of Bangladesh, surrounded on all sides by large estates. Roads wind between hills covered in tea bushes, shaded by tall trees, where women pluck leaves into baskets on their backs. Walks or cycle rides through the gardens reveal tea-worker villages, small temples and lakes. The Bangladesh Tea Research Institute is also nearby.
blocks: How to get there
Train or bus from Dhaka to Srimangal (about 4–5 hours), then explore by CNG, bicycle or on foot.
Good to know
Respect estate rules and the privacy of workers' homes. Leeches appear in the rainy season.

glance: Wholesale lemon arats at Srimangal's old and new bazar, and Bhanugachh, Adampur and Shamshernagar bazars in Kamalganj
srimangal-lemon.desc: Between the tea estates of Srimangal and Kamalganj are hillside lemon gardens, and this is the country's biggest lemon-growing area. Wholesalers at the Srimangal bazars buy lakhs of taka worth of lemons a day and send them across the country. Visitors often pick up a bag of big, juicy lemons along with their tea.

seven-layer-tea.desc: Seven-layer tea was created in Srimangal and became a must-try for visitors. Different teas, milk and spices are layered by density so that each band stays separate in the glass, from pale to dark. Each layer has its own taste, from sweet and milky to spiced and strong. The recipe is kept secret by its makers.

glance: Baruna Ghat bazar in Kalapur union, Srimangal (about 7–10 am); rice hotels in Srimangal town
hail-haor-fish.desc: Hail Haor, just west of Srimangal, is a big wetland full of native fish. Each morning fishermen bring their catch to Baruna Ghat bazar on the haor's edge, where boal, rui, katla, shol, koi, magur, puti and mola are sold by auction for a couple of hours. Traders then carry the fish into Srimangal's markets and rice hotels, where you can have it as a curry or fry with rice.

hakaluki-haor.desc: Hakaluki is a vast haor basin made up of many beels, spreading across parts of Moulvibazar and Sylhet. In the rainy season it fills into a great sheet of water with villages on raised mounds. In winter, as the water falls, thousands of migratory ducks and waders arrive, and fishermen work the remaining beels. Swamp trees such as hijal and koroch dot the landscape.
blocks: How to get there
Reach Kulaura or Juri by bus or train, then hire local transport and a boat.
Good to know
For birds, go between December and February with a local guide and binoculars. Life jackets on boats.

hamham-waterfall.desc: Hamham lies deep in the Rajkandi forest of Kamalganj, near the Tripura border, and only became widely known in the 2010s. The trek in takes a few hours each way, following stream beds and steep, slippery hill paths through bamboo and jungle. At the end, the water falls in a tall white veil down a rock face into a shallow pool.
blocks: How to get there
From Srimangal take a jeep or CNG to Kalabon para in Kamalganj, then trek with a local guide.
Good to know
Hire a local guide, start early, carry water and a bamboo stick, and wear leech socks in the rains. Turn back if streams are flooding.
